1. No proper pregnancy assessment before starting 🚩

Were you asked about your trimester, medical history, pain, pelvic pressure, leaking, exercise history or current symptoms before being added in? 🤔
Because pregnancy exercise should never be “one-size-fits-all.”

2. Too many pregnant women, barely any individual attention 🚩

If the instructor is handling a huge batch, are they really able to observe your breathing, posture, alignment or exercise form properly? 👀

Correct cueing & observation matter so much during pregnancy.

3. Every pregnant woman doing the exact same workout 🚩

A first trimester mom with nausea, a third trimester mom with pelvic pain & someone who was strength training pre-pregnancy will all need very different exercise approaches. Your program should reflect that!!

4. “Prenatal” classes with no real women’s health expertise 🚩

Pregnancy fitness is not just modified workouts. A qualified prenatal professional should understand pregnancy physiology, pelvic health, pressure management, common symptoms & when modifications are medically needed.

5. No changes based on your posture, strength or symptoms 🚩

Back pain, pelvic girdle pain, heaviness, fatigue, rib flare, balance changes, coning or leaking during workouts shouldn’t be ignored 

Your exercises should adapt to your changing body.. not the other way around.

A good prenatal class should make you feel safe, supported, educated & confidently guided through pregnancy 💗

✔️ Pre conception tests:
haemoglobin, thyroid profile, vitamin levels, blood sugar, infections & more
✔️ Pre conception counselling:

for better maternal & fetal health 🥗

Before it became what we know as Pilates today, it was called “Contrology” a method created by Joseph Pilates.

His journey shaped the method.
As a child, he struggled with multiple health issues, which led him to deeply study the body, movement, and strength. During World War I, he worked with injured soldiers, using spring-based resistance to help them recover.. laying the foundation for what we now know as Pilates equipment.

When he later opened his studio in New York, Contrology became a space for healing, strength, and movement, especially among dancers and performers.

Contrology wasn’t just exercise.
It was a system of movement built on:

• breath
• control
• precision
• flow
• centering (the powerhouse)
• alignment

Every movement had intention.
Every transition had purpose.

He believed:
“It is the mind itself which builds the body.”

Over the years, Pilates has evolved & that evolution is important too.

Today, we understand more about biomechanics, rehabilitation, pelvic health, and the nervous system. This allows us to adapt the method for modern bodies.. making it more accessible, therapeutic, and relevant.

We modify. We personalise. We meet the body where it is. But the essence remains.

At its core, Pilates still teaches you how to move.
How to find your neutral spine,
engage your deep core,
move with control over momentum,
and connect breath with movement.

And that’s why I LOVEEEEE Pilates 😍

Because it goes beyond a workout.
It builds awareness that stays with you.. in how you move, sit, stand & live.

Simple, but never easy. Subtle, but deeply powerful.

On World Pilates Day, this is just a reminder of where it all began & why it still matters 🤍

You don’t need every supplement in pregnancy.
You need the right ones 💊✨

Most women are told what to take…
but not what is actually essential vs optional 👇🏽 

🌸 Must-have (usually prescribed as supplements)
These are difficult to meet through diet alone and are almost always needed:

• Folic Acid – critical for baby’s brain & spine (especially early pregnancy)
• Iron – prevents anemia and supports increased blood demand
• Calcium + Vitamin D – baby’s bones + maternal bone protection
• Vitamin B12 – baby’s brain & nerve development (very important in vegetarians)

✨ Can be managed through diet (supplement if needed)

• Protein – from dal, dairy, eggs, nuts
• Omega-3 (DHA) – from walnuts, seeds (supplements if intake is low)

⚖️ Only if required (based on symptoms/reports)

• Magnesium – for cramps, sleep issues
• Zinc – if deficiency or low immunity
• Iodine – usually covered through iodized salt/prenatal vitamins

🚫 What you should NOT do:
Don’t take multiple supplements randomly
Don’t copy someone else’s prescription
Don’t assume “more is better”

💡 The right way:
These are the nutrients your body needs, 
but your dosage and supplements should be personalised

⚠️ Always consult your doctor before starting any supplement

This pregnancy habit is not just “good for you”… it’s building your baby’s brain 🧠👶🏻 

There’s a powerful protein your body produces called
Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor

And it plays a key role in brain development.

🧠 What does BDNF actually do?

BDNF helps:
• Brain cells grow (neurogenesis)
• Form stronger connections (synapses)
• Function efficiently

👉🏼 In simple terms: it supports how the brain is built and wired

🤰🏻 Why does this matter in pregnancy?

Your baby’s brain is developing rapidly in the womb.

Higher BDNF levels are associated with:
• Better neuronal growth
• Improved brain connectivity
• Stronger foundation for learning & memory

🚶🏻‍♀️Where does exercise come in?

Research shows that exercise increases BDNF levels

When you move:
• Blood flow to the brain improves
• Oxygen & nutrients increase
• Your body signals the brain to release more BDNF

👉🏼 Creating a more supportive environment for your baby’s brain development

💛 Benefits for both mom & baby

For baby 👶🏻 
• Supports brain development
• Enhances neural connections

For mom 🤰🏻 
• Improves mood
• Reduces stress & anxiety
• Supports mental well-being

Exercise in pregnancy is not just about weight or fitness.
It is a neuroprotective and neurodevelopmental tool benefiting both maternal and fetal brain health.

📚 References 

• Erickson KI et al. Exercise training increases size of hippocampus and improves memory (PNAS, 2011)
• ACOG Committee Opinion No. 804: Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period
• Huang T et al. The effects of exercise on BDNF levels in humans (Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 2014)

🚨 Newsflash: Debilitating pain is NOT normal! 🚨

Train SMARTER, not HARDER!💪🏽

Let’s decode how to train during different phases of MENSTRUAL CYCLE to attain optimal fitness!🩸

➡️Menstrual Phase (Days 1-5):
During the menstrual phase, estrogen and progesterone levels are at their lowest. This is a time for gentle exercises like Stretching, yoga, pilates and walking. Opt for activities that provide relief from menstrual discomfort and promote relaxation.

➡️Follicular Phase (Days 6-13):
As the body transitions into the follicular phase, estrogen starts to rise. This phase is characterized by increased energy and stamina. Engage in more intense workouts such as cardio, strength training, taking advantage of the heightened estrogen levels.

➡️Ovulatory Phase (Day 14):
The ovulatory phase sees a peak in estrogen, contributing to improved strength and endurance. Embrace challenging workouts during this phase, including HIIT (High Intensity Interval Training), Strength training or Weight lifting. Leverage the elevated energy levels for more demanding fitness routines.

➡️Luteal Phase (Days 15-28):
Moving into the luteal phase, estrogen decreases while progesterone rises. This phase may bring PMS symptoms and increased susceptibility to muscle soreness. Opt for stability-focused exercises like Pilates, Yoga, walking or swimming. Mindful workouts can help manage stress and support the body through hormonal fluctuations during the luteal phase.

‼️Remember, these are general guidelines, and individual responses to hormonal changes can vary. Listening to your body and adjusting your workout routine accordingly is key to optimizing the benefits of cycle syncing for your fitness journey✨

That sharp pain in the front of your pelvis isn’t “just pregnancy.” Here’s what’s actually happening…

If turning in bed, getting out of the car, climbing stairs, or even walking suddenly causes a sharp pain in the front of your pelvis, you’re not alone.

This is often Pregnancy-Related Pelvic Girdle Pain (PGP) or specifically Pubic Symphysis Dysfunction (PSD).. a condition that affects around 1 in 5 pregnant women. Yet, many moms are told it’s “normal” and are left struggling through everyday activities without knowing why it hurts.

Here’s the science behind it 👇🏽 

During pregnancy, hormones like relaxin increase ligament laxity to prepare your body for childbirth. As a result, the pubic symphysis, the joint that connects the two halves of your pelvis.. becomes slightly more mobile.

When one leg moves differently from the other, such as while rolling in bed, stepping out of a car, climbing stairs, or standing on one leg, increased shear forces act across this joint. This can lead to pain, tenderness, and a feeling of pelvic instability.

The good news? 
While this condition is common, persistent pain shouldn’t be ignored. The right physiotherapy, movement modifications, and pregnancy-safe exercises can make a significant difference and help you move more comfortably.

🚨 Pubic pain while getting out of bed during pregnancy?🤰🏻 

That sharp pain at the front of your pelvis isn’t “just part of pregnancy.”

During pregnancy, hormones such as relaxin help prepare your body for birth by increasing ligament laxity. As your baby grows, the load on your pelvis also increases. Together, these changes can make the pubic symphysis (the joint at the front of your pelvis) more sensitive and less stable, especially during movements where one leg moves independently.

That’s why getting out of bed the wrong way can make it worse.

❌ Avoid:
• Twisting your pelvis
• Moving one leg at a time
• Letting your knees separate
• Sitting up by twisting

✅ Instead:
• Keep your knees together
• Log roll onto your side
• Move your shoulders and hips together
• Use your arms to push yourself up
• Bring both legs off the bed together

The goal is to reduce shearing forces across the pubic symphysis and keep your pelvis moving as one unit.

If turning in bed, getting out of the car, climbing stairs, standing on one leg, or even walking has become painful, you could be experiencing Pregnancy-Related Pelvic Girdle Pain (PGP) or Symphysis Pubis Dysfunction (SPD).

During pregnancy, hormonal changes increase ligament laxity while your growing baby changes your body’s centre of gravity and the way forces are transferred through the pelvis. When the muscles that support the pelvis aren’t working together efficiently, the pubic symphysis can become irritated and painful.

The good news? The right exercises can help.

Targeted strengthening of your glutes, deep core, hip stabilisers, pelvic floor, and inner thigh muscles can improve pelvic stability, reduce excessive stress across the pubic symphysis, and help you move with less pain and more confidence.

Pain during pregnancy is common but that doesn’t mean you have to simply put up with it.
